slides.title: The First Fundamental Form
slides.notes: Open the lecture by presenting the first fundamental form as the measuring rule that lives on a surface patch. The point is not to memorize three letters, but to see how dot products of tangent vectors become a compact local ledger. This chapter asks how far that ledger goes: it computes lengths, angles, areas, and decides what different surface maps preserve.

slides.title: What Can Be Read From One Quadratic Form?
slides.notes: This slide sets up the central translation: a parametrized patch gives two tangent directions, and their dot products assemble the Gram matrix. Emphasize that \(E,F,G\) are not arbitrary coefficients; they record the actual Euclidean lengths and mutual angle of \(\sigma_u\) and \(\sigma_v\). The class should read the diagram from left to right: a coordinate velocity becomes a physical tangent vector whose length is measured by \(M\).

slides.title: Five Uses Of The Same Data
slides.notes: Give students the shape of the lecture before entering the formulas. Each topic reuses the same metric matrix, but asks for a different invariant: exact metric preservation, scalar rescaling, determinant preservation, or distance on the sphere. This road map prevents the chapter from feeling like a sequence of unrelated examples; it is one measuring device used in several modes.

slides.title: Metric Coefficients As Local Rulers
slides.notes: This section divider is a conceptual pause: the class is leaving the visual patch and concentrating on the metric as a local ruler. Stress that the coordinate pair \((du,dv)\) by itself has no physical meaning until the surface tells us how the coordinate grid is stretched and sheared. The matrix is the compact object that performs that conversion.

slides.title: The Gram Matrix Of A Patch
slides.notes: Introduce \(M\) as a Gram matrix, which helps students connect this chapter to linear algebra they already know. The ellipse is useful because it shows the metric as an anisotropic measuring rule: different coordinate velocities can have the same physical speed, and the tilt records the cross term \(F\). The warning prepares students for a common mistake, which is to read orthogonality from the parameter domain instead of from the dot product on the surface.

slides.title: The Determinant Measures The Grid Cell
slides.notes: This slide isolates the determinant because it will become the decisive quantity in Archimedes' theorem and in equiareal maps. The parallelogram picture makes the algebraic expression \(EG-F^2\) feel less mysterious: it is simply the square of the area spanned by the two tangent vectors. Point out that preserving determinant is weaker than preserving the whole matrix, which is why area can survive while angles and lengths change.

slides.title: Metric Speed Along A Coordinate Curve
slides.notes: Here the first fundamental form becomes an operational formula for curve length. The important teaching move is to compare the coordinate curve with its image on the surface: the same parameter \(t\) is used, but the metric supplies the physical speed. The final check reassures students that the formula is not a new assumption; it is the chain rule plus the dot products already stored in \(M\).

slides.title: The Cylinder Keeps The Plane Metric
slides.notes: The cylinder example is the cleanest way to separate bending from stretching. Even though the strip and cylinder look different in three-dimensional space, the tangent dot products agree with those of the original coordinate plane. Use this to define local isometry concretely: the map preserves the entire first fundamental form, not merely the appearance of a grid.

slides.title: Three Preservation Tests, One Matrix
slides.notes: Pause here to make the classification logic explicit. All three tests compare metric matrices, but they demand different levels of agreement. This framing is especially helpful before stereographic projection and Archimedes' theorem, because those examples are often remembered visually while their actual metric behavior is more precise.

slides.title: What Each Map Type Preserves
slides.notes: Use the table to keep students from conflating the three preservation words. Isometry is a full inner-product statement, conformality keeps angles because every tangent length is scaled by the same local factor, and equiareality only constrains the area density. The two boxes at the bottom explain why the implications run in one direction: full matrix equality implies determinant equality, but not conversely.

slides.title: Stereographic Projection Scales Evenly
slides.notes: Stereographic projection is the chapter's model for conformality. The formula shows that the pulled-back metric is a scalar multiple of the flat metric, and the scalar depends on radius. Ask students to inspect the two crossing curves: the angle behavior is protected because every tangent direction at a point is multiplied by the same local factor, even though size changes from place to place.

slides.title: Archimedes Swaps The Metric Coefficients
slides.notes: Present Archimedes' theorem as a determinant computation rather than as a purely spatial surprise. The matrices differ by swapping where the \(\cos^2\theta\) factor appears, so tangent directions are distorted differently. Yet their determinants agree, which is exactly what the area element sees; this is the chapter's equiareal mechanism in a classical setting.

slides.title: Spherical Geometry From The Same Metric Habit
slides.notes: This section moves from local measurement to global-looking formulas on the unit sphere. The key message is that spherical distance is still metric length, but the minimizing curves are great-circle arcs. The dot-product formula for distance is convenient because it packages that metric length as a central angle between unit vectors.

slides.title: Great-Circle Length Is A Central Angle
slides.notes: Students often confuse the Euclidean chord with the spherical distance, so explicitly contrast them. The chord is a straight line through space, while the metric distance on the sphere is measured along the surface. The dot product formula is powerful because it computes that surface length from ambient coordinates without choosing a latitude-longitude chart.

slides.title: Angles Live In Tangent Planes
slides.notes: This slide translates a spherical triangle into computable metric data. The side lengths come from central angles, but the vertex angles are not angles between chords; they are angles between tangent directions to the great circles at the vertex. The spherical excess formula then turns that angle data into area, showing another way the first fundamental form controls measurement on the sphere.

slides.title: Classify A Map By Pulling Back Its Metric
slides.notes: The applied lab turns the definitions into a repeatable procedure. Start with the strongest condition because equality of matrices immediately gives all the other first-order measurements, then relax to scalar multiple and determinant checks. This is a useful computational habit: a visual map may look convincing, but the pullback metric tells exactly what has been preserved.

slides.title: Three Examples, Three Outcomes
slides.notes: This slide consolidates the examples into the diagnostic language students should carry forward. The cylinder, stereographic projection, and Archimedes map are deliberately placed side by side because they satisfy different matrix conditions. Encourage students to state both the classification and the evidence; the evidence is always a relation between metric matrices or their determinants.

slides.title: The Chapter In One Metric Ledger
slides.notes: Close by returning to the chapter question from the title slide. The first fundamental form is the local metric tensor of a surface patch, and the entire lecture has been a tour of what that tensor can compute. The final diagram should leave students with a compact mental model: once \(M\) is known, many geometric questions become precise matrix questions.
